title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

content.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

blocks.text: Given the head of a linked list, remove the n-th node FROM THE END of the list, and return its head.

blocks.caption: A fast pointer starts n nodes ahead; walking both together lands slow right before the target

blocks.text: Given a linked list and an integer n, remove the node that is exactly n positions from the end of the list, and return the resulting list's head.

blocks.title: Analogy: Keeping a Fixed Following Distance in a Line of Cars
blocks.text: Like one car (fast) starting exactly n car-lengths ahead of another car (slow) in a line of traffic, both then driving forward together at the same speed, maintaining that exact n-car gap the whole time. The moment the lead car reaches the very end of the line, the trailing car must be sitting exactly n cars back from the end, precisely the position needed to remove.

blocks.caption: A fixed n-node gap between two pointers lands the trailing one exactly before the target

blocks.text: Before counting the list's total length first (to convert "n from the end" into "some position from the start"), notice that a fixed gap between two pointers achieves the same result in a single combined pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: "The n-th node from the end" is hard to identify directly while walking forward from the head, since the list's total length isn't known in advance without a separate counting pass.

Observation 2: If a "fast" pointer is advanced n steps ahead of a "slow" pointer FIRST, then advancing both together (one step each) maintains that exact same n-node gap between them throughout.

Observation 3: By the time fast reaches the very last node (or one past it, depending on exact implementation), slow must be sitting exactly n nodes behind it, which is precisely the node needing removal (or, using a dummy head and stopping slow one step earlier, the node just BEFORE the target, ready to skip over it).

Observation 4: Using a dummy head (as in other removal problems) uniformly handles the case where the target node to remove is the actual head of the list.

Recognizing that establishing a FIXED gap between two pointers converts "count from the end" into a problem solvable in a single forward pass is a broadly reusable technique whenever a position is specified relative to a sequence's end rather than its start.

This is the classic two-pointer "fixed gap" technique: advancing one pointer a set number of steps ahead first, then moving both together, to find a position measured from the end of a sequence in a single pass.
First walk through the list once to count its total length, then walk through it a second time to reach the node just before the target.

items: Walk through the list once, counting the total number of nodes.
Compute the target's position from the start (length - n), then walk through the list a second time to reach the node just before that position, and skip over the target.

codes.python:
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    length = 0
    node = head
    while node:
        length += 1                                                        # first pass: count the total number of nodes
        node = node.next
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    cur = dummy
    for _ in range(length - n):                                            # walk to just before the node that needs removing
        cur = cur.next
    cur.next = cur.next.next                                               # skip over the target node directly
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
    result = remove_nth_from_end(head, 2)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The dummy head handles the case where the target node to remove is the actual head, uniformly with every other position.
The first pass counts nodes without modifying anything, purely to determine the list's total length.
The second pass walks exactly (length - n) steps from the dummy to land just before the target, ready to skip over it.

blocks.text: The list length is correctly counted, and the target node is correctly identified and removed, so the result is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(L), where L is the list's length, across two separate passes.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: requiring two separate passes through the list (one to count, one to reach the target) ignores that a single coordinated pass, using two pointers maintaining a fixed gap, can find and remove the exact same target node directly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force needs two separate passes. Instead, use a dummy head and two pointers, fast and slow, both starting at dummy. Advance fast n steps ahead first, establishing a fixed gap. Then advance both fast and slow together, one step each, until fast reaches the last node. At that point, slow sits exactly one node before the target, ready to skip over it directly.

Initialize dummy pointing to head, with fast and slow both starting at dummy. Advance fast n times. Then, while fast.next is not null, advance both fast and slow by one step each. Once the loop ends, set slow.next = slow.next.next, skipping the target node. Return dummy.next.
Establish a fixed n-node gap between two pointers, then advance both together until the leading one reaches the end.

blocks.text: slow sits at the node valued 3, so slow.next (valued 4) is the target; skipping it gives [1,2,3,5], matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    fast = dummy
    slow = dummy
    for _ in range(n):
        fast = fast.next                                                    # advance fast n steps ahead first, establishing a fixed gap
    while fast.next:
        fast = fast.next                                                    # advance both pointers together, maintaining the same gap
        slow = slow.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next                                              # slow now sits exactly before the target; skip over it
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
    result = remove_nth_from_end(head, 2)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(L), a single combined pass through the list.
Space: O(1) extra, using only the dummy node and 2 pointers.

Advancing fast n steps ahead first establishes a fixed gap of exactly n nodes between fast and slow. Since both pointers then advance at the same rate (one step each), this gap never changes throughout the rest of the walk. By the time fast reaches the last node (fast.next becomes null), slow, being exactly n nodes behind, must be sitting exactly one node before the true target (the n-th from the end), ready to skip over it directly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["fast.next becomes null (fast has reached the last node)","slow is now exactly one node before the target; skip over it via slow.next = slow.next.next"]]}

items: The dummy head ensures slow can correctly skip over the target even if the target is the true head of the list.
fast is advanced n times BEFORE the main loop begins, establishing the fixed gap upfront.
The main loop condition (fast.next != null) stops at exactly the right moment, since it checks fast.next rather than fast itself, correctly positioning slow just before the target rather than at it.

blocks.text: The fixed-gap two-pointer technique is a broadly reusable way to locate a position measured from the END of a sequence in a single pass, without first needing to know the sequence's total length.

items: Advancing fast n+1 times (or n-1 times) instead of exactly n, causing slow to land one position off from where it should be.
Not using a dummy head, missing the case where the target to remove is the true head of the list.
Using the wrong loop condition (checking fast instead of fast.next), causing slow to land ON the target instead of just before it.

items: Explicitly explain why advancing fast n steps ahead FIRST (before the main loop) establishes and maintains a fixed gap, since walking through this logic carefully is exactly what demonstrates true understanding of the technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find/remove a node measured from the END of a linked list, in a single pass" points toward the fixed-gap two-pointer technique: advance one pointer ahead first, then move both together.

items: How would you find the n-th node from the end WITHOUT removing it? Use the exact same fixed-gap technique, but without the dummy head's skip step; simply return slow once fast reaches the end (no dummy needed if just reading, not removing).

How would you remove multiple nodes measured from the end, given several different n values? Sort the n values, and either make multiple passes or track multiple simultaneous "slow" pointers, each launched at the appropriate offset.

What if the list's length were needed for OTHER purposes too? In that case, a single length-counting pass followed by direct indexing (the brute force shown here) might be equally reasonable, sharing that computed length across multiple uses.

The fixed-gap two-pointer technique, a distinct cousin of the equal-speed slow/fast technique seen in Middle of the Linked List and Linked List Cycle, here using an initial HEAD START instead of a speed difference to establish the needed positional relationship.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(L) time (two passes), O(1) space.
Optimized (fixed-gap two pointers): O(L) time (one pass), O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Fixed-gap two-pointer technique: advance one pointer n steps ahead first, then move both together
Core Idea: A fixed n-node gap between two pointers means the trailing pointer sits exactly n nodes from the end when the leading one reaches it
Time: O(L)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Establishing a fixed positional gap between two pointers converts "measured from the end" into a single-pass problem, without needing the list's length in advance
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Advance fast n steps first; then move both together until fast.next is null; slow.next is the target
